definitions.explanation: The Buddhist concept that all things are transient and nothing remains unchanged. A fundamental idea in Japanese aesthetics and philosophy, closely tied to the appreciation of fleeting beauty.

examples.japanese: {人生|じんせい}の{無常|むじょう}を{感|かん}じる。
examples.english: I feel the impermanence of life.

examples.japanese: {散|ち}りゆく{桜|さくら}に{無常|むじょう}を{感|かん}じるのは{日本人|にほんじん}ならではの{感性|かんせい}だ。
examples.english: Feeling impermanence in falling cherry blossoms is a sensibility unique to the Japanese.

examples.japanese: 「{祇園精舎|ぎおんしょうじゃ}の{鐘|かね}の{声|こえ}、{諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}の{響|ひび}きあり」は、『{平家物語|へいけものがたり}』の{冒頭|ぼうとう}として{有名|ゆうめい}だ。
examples.english: "The sound of the bells of Gion Shoja echoes the impermanence of all things" is famous as the opening of The Tale of the Heike.

notes:
CULTURAL NOTE:
{無常|むじょう} is one of the most important concepts in Japanese culture, originating from Buddhist philosophy. The idea that all phenomena are transient pervades Japanese literature, art, and aesthetics — from the opening of the {平家物語|へいけものがたり} (The Tale of the Heike) to the appreciation of {桜|さくら} (cherry blossoms) precisely because they fall.

KEY EXPRESSION:
{諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう} (all things are impermanent) is a core Buddhist teaching and one of the most widely known four-character idioms in Japanese.

RELATED WORDS:
- {無常|むじょう}{観|かん}: a worldview based on impermanence
- {無常|むじょう}の{風|かぜ}: the "wind of impermanence" (poetic expression for death)
- {儚|はかな}い: fleeting, ephemeral (an aesthetic concept closely related to {無常|むじょう})

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {無常|むじょう}を{感|かん}じる: to feel impermanence
- {諸行無常|しょぎょうむじょう}: all things are impermanent
- {無常|むじょう}{観|かん}: sense of impermanence
- {世|よ}の{無常|むじょう}: the transience of the world
